claims.claim: The highest-leverage structural defect is that max_budget is reused as a per-call cap on every LLM invocation rather than as a cumulative cap across a run. WorkflowContext.call_llm_structured does kwargs.setdefault('max_budget', self.max_budget) on every call, and the deliberation builder passes the same scalar into every agent and synthesis invocation. With the CLI default --max-budget=8.0 and max_rounds=5, worst-case real spend is (2*5+1)=11 calls * $8 = $88 per debate — and there is no chassis-level counter that detects this. Convergence false-positives produce a wrong answer; budget-cap leakage produces runaway cost, which is the more dangerous shipped failure mode at the user's stated 'max_rounds > 5' question.

The convergence detector is not just polite-trusting (peer's framing) — it is structurally weaker than peer claim a1 states, because `agreed_with_peer` is a `list[str]` of free-text strings the same agent authors in the same response, and `detect_convergence` only checks set inclusion (`other_claim_ids.issubset(agreed_set)`), not that the listed IDs are actually current peer IDs. An agent can also silently retire a claim it raised last round; since the check inspects only `latest_positions`, dropped claims disappear from the convergence test entirely. Both failure modes converge spuriously without any politeness on the agent's part.

Round-1 is structurally non-independent because the LangGraph edges hard-wire agent_a -> agent_b -> round_increment, the entry_point is agent_a, and agent_a's position is written into latest_positions before agent_b's node fires. Therefore at round_num=1, agent_b's `peer_latest = latest.get(agent_a_name)` is populated with agent_a's just-written initial position. This is deterministic from the graph, not a policy choice — exactly what peer a3 claims, and the edge wiring in build_deliberation_workflow proves it.

The deliberation chassis is missing the TaskFamily/profile extension point the duet has, despite the module docstring explicitly promising 'deliberation can also be specialized by profile when domain-specific Position fields are needed.' There is no DeliberationFamily, no deliberation registry, and Position is not subclassable through the builder — `build_deliberation_workflow` accepts no `task_family` parameter and hard-codes the generic `Position` model in both agent nodes and synthesis. The duet has duet_registry.py + TaskFamily and `build_duet_workflow(task_family=...)`; deliberation has no analog. This is the most concrete structural inconsistency between the two siblings.

Synthesis is a separate context-bloat failure mode independent of convergence drift: the synthesis prompt dumps the full chronological position_history via json.dumps without truncation or summarization, into a single LLM call that reuses the same per-call max_budget. At max_rounds=5 with two agents, that's ~10 Position blobs (each with claims + evidence content_snippet + disagreements) in one prompt — so 'context bloat' from the user's question is real, just located in synthesis rather than in per-round agent prompts (which correctly only see peer_latest + own_prior).

`evidence_path` is a single free-text string with zero structural sub-grammar — it accepts 'docs/plans/...md#section', 'file.py:LL-LL', or 'because I said so' equivalently. The schema's only enforcement is presence, not format. The duet profile `plan_doc_review` already uses 'list every cited file:line ... you could not open or whose claimed content you could not confirm' language as a prompt-time check, but neither workflow has a chassis-level path/line validator. Peer claim a2 is correct that presence != truthfulness; I add that even *format* isn't enforced, so an automated verifier doesn't have to do semantic checking to add value — even a file-exists check would catch most gaming.

disagreed_with_peer.my_counterclaim: I agree the convergence rule is unsound (see my b2 which extends the diagnosis beyond politeness to free-text-ID gaming and silent claim retirement), but I disagree that it is the highest-risk flaw. Per-call budget reuse (b1) is more dangerous because a polite false-convergence at most ships a wrong synthesis; an uncapped budget at max_rounds=5+ ships an $80+ bill silently. The user's prompt explicitly asks 'what fails first at max_rounds > 5?' and the answer is cost, not correctness — convergence-audit is #2, not #1, on leverage.

Peer says 'first structural failure is convergence drift plus synthesis-history scaling, not per-turn prompt bloat.' I half-agree: per-turn agent prompts correctly bound their context to peer_latest + own_prior (deliberate.py:329-352), so peer is right there. But synthesis IS a context-bloat failure mode, not just history scaling — the synthesis node calls one LLM with the entire position_history serialized via json.dumps and a per-call budget cap. At max_rounds=5, ~10 Position blobs (each with content_snippets) hit one prompt. So both 'cost runaway' (b1) and 'synthesis context bloat' (b5) fail before convergence drift bites; peer's ordering misranks them.

Peer says 'the missing piece is not a third user-facing workflow but a reusable verifier/adjudicator stage.' I agree a verifier is valuable but disagree on framing: the more immediate structural debt is that the deliberation chassis has no TaskFamily-style profile extension point at all, despite the deliberate.py:24-32 docstring promising one. The duet ships duet_registry.py + TaskFamily; deliberation hard-codes generic Position and offers no task_family kwarg to build_deliberation_workflow. Add the profile hook first; then 'verifier' becomes a registered profile stage rather than a forked code path. Peer's verifier idea is right; the build order is wrong.

open_questions: Does llm_client.core.client enforce a per-trace_id cumulative spend cap at the kernel layer that would mask the workflow-layer leakage in b1? If yes, b1 downgrades from 'high' to 'warn'; needs a Read of llm_client/core/client.py.

If a DeliberationFamily extension point were added (b4), should the verifier/adjudicator stage peer proposes in a5 be a registered TaskFamily-style hook rather than a hard-coded third pattern? That would let plan_doc_review and twin_update plug in domain-specific verifiers without forking the chassis.

Does the convergence detector handle the case where `agreed_with_peer` contains duplicate claim_ids or fabricated IDs that don't appear in the peer's claims at all? Current `set(...).issubset(...)` ignores garbage entries — should fabricated IDs be a stalling signal?
reviewer_summary:
Ranking by leverage (mine, defended explicitly against peer's): (1) Fix the per-call budget reuse in WorkflowContext (b1) — this is the *only* defect that turns 'max_rounds > 5' from a quality concern into a financial-safety concern, and the user's prompt asked specifically about max_rounds > 5. (2) Replace self-reported `agreed_with_peer` coverage with chassis-owned claim lineage that detects silent claim retirement, not just politeness (b2; extends peer a1). (3) Fix true round-1 independence by making agent_a and agent_b round-1 nodes parallel rather than sequential edges (b3; agrees with peer a3). (4) Add a DeliberationFamily/registry to match duet (b4; disagreement with peer a5 — extension point first, verifier as a registered stage second). (5) Truncate or summarize synthesis history (b5). (6) Validate evidence_path format at the chassis level — even file-exists is a win (b6; extends peer a2). The single highest-priority next improvement is converting `WorkflowContext.max_budget` from a per-call setdefault into a cumulative spend ledger keyed by trace_id, with a hard stop when the run total approaches the cap; this is small, mechanical, kernel-adjacent, and it gates everything else — a polite agent merely produces a bad synthesis, but an uncapped one burns dollars per debate. Peer's adjudicator/verifier stage is the right *second* move once cost-safety is real.</reviewer_summary>
